What is boundary value analysis?.raw:
Boundary value analysis (BVA) is a black-box testing technique that designs test cases around the edges of the input domain. The idea is that programmers most often make mistakes at the boundaries of a range — the minimum, the maximum, and the values immediately inside and outside them [1].

- For a field accepting integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA suggests testing 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101 [1].
- The classic three-point rule tests the minimum, minimum minus one, minimum plus one, plus the maximum, maximum minus one and maximum plus one — giving six test cases [1].
- BVA pairs naturally with equivalence partitioning: EP first divides the input domain into classes of values that should behave the same, and BVA then picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors are most likely to hide [1].

Equivalence partitioning, or EP, divides the input domain of a program into
equivalence classes: groups of values the program is expected to treat identically.
Testing one representative value from each class is assumed to reveal the same faults
as testing every member of the class, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases.

Partitions are drawn from both valid and invalid inputs. For an age field that accepts

strategy. The resulting test suite is much smaller than exhaustive testing but still
covers every behaviourally distinct category of input.

passages.title: Statement and Branch Coverage
passages.heading: Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
passages.text:
Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

Branch coverage is often called decision coverage. It subsumes statement coverage:
reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.

What is equivalence partitioning?.raw:
Equivalence partitioning (EP) is a black-box technique that divides a program's input domain into equivalence classes: groups of values the program should treat identically. The idea is that testing one representative value from each class should reveal the same faults as testing every member, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases you need [1].

- Partitions come from both valid and invalid inputs. For an age field accepting 0 to 120, the valid class is 0 to 120, and the invalid classes are negative values and values above 120. A complete test set samples at least one value from each class [1].

- EP pairs naturally with boundary value analysis: EP splits the domain into classes, then BVA picks values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors tend to hide [2].

What is the difference between statement.raw:
Statement coverage and branch coverage differ in what they require a test suite to exercise.

- **Statement coverage** measures the share of executable statements that a suite runs. Full statement coverage means every line of code has been executed at least once [1].
- **Branch coverage** (also called decision coverage) requires every decision, such as an if or a switch, to take both its true and false outcome at least once. Even an if with no else clause needs one test that skips the body and one that enters it [1].

Strength: statement coverage is the weakest structural criterion, because a suite can reach full statement coverage while still missing many bugs in decisions. Branch coverage is stronger, and it subsumes statement coverage: full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, since every statement lies on some branch [1].

One limit to note: a suite with full branch coverage but not condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on combinations of several conditions inside a single decision [1].

How do boundary value analysis and equiv.raw:
Boundary value analysis (BVA) and equivalence partitioning (EP) are complementary black-box techniques, and they're usually used together.

- EP goes first: it divides the input domain into equivalence classes, groups of values the program should treat identically. Testing one representative value per class is assumed to catch the same faults as testing every value, which cuts the number of test cases dramatically [2]. Classes come from both valid and invalid inputs. For an age field accepting 0 to 120, the valid class is 0 to 120 and the invalid classes are negative values and values above 120 [2].
- BVA then refines where you pick values: instead of any representative, it targets the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors are most likely to hide [1]. For a field accepting integers 1 to 100, BVA suggests 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101, following the three-point rule (min, min-1, min+1, max, max-1, max+1), which gives six test cases [1].
- So EP tells you which classes to cover; BVA tells you which values inside or just outside each class are worth testing [1].

When a program has several inputs, EP treats each input's classes independently and then combines representative values, usually with an all-combinations or pairwise strategy, so the suite stays far smaller than exhaustive testing while still covering every behaviourally distinct category of input [2].

study_guide:quantum entanglement (off-sy.raw:
## Quantum Entanglement

This isn't covered in your course materials, so here's a general explanation:

- Quantum entanglement is a relationship between two or more quantum particles whose combined state cannot be described by describing each particle separately, no matter how far apart they are.
- Entangled particles are described by a single shared state. For two qubits, a well-known example is the Bell state, written in plain text as (|00> + |11>)/sqrt(2), where the two particles are always measured in matching states.
- Before measurement, neither particle has a definite value for the measured property. Measurement outcomes are correlated, and those correlations can be stronger than any classical shared-randomness model can reproduce; this is what Bell tests and Bell inequalities check.
- Entanglement does not allow faster-than-light communication. Each side's local measurement results look random on their own; the correlation only becomes visible when the two sets of results are compared through an ordinary (slower-than-light) channel.
- Entanglement is a physical resource rather than just a curiosity. It underlies quantum teleportation, quantum key distribution, dense coding, and is used as a resource in quantum computing and quantum error correction.
- Entanglement is fragile: interactions with the environment cause decoherence, which degrades entangled states, so experiments and devices rely on isolation, low temperatures, and error correction.
- A useful conceptual caution: entanglement is not the same as superposition (one particle in several states at once) or as classical correlation (for example, two gloves in separate boxes). It is the non-separable joint state that distinguishes it.

Note: your course passages cover software testing topics (boundary value analysis, equivalence partitioning, statement and branch coverage), so they do not contain material on this topic. The points above are general background and carry no citations from your course readings.

Which six values does boundary value ana.raw:
For a field that accepts integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA tests these six values [1]:

- 0 — minimum minus one
- 1 — the minimum
- 2 — minimum plus one
- 99 — maximum minus one
- 100 — the maximum
- 101 — maximum plus one

This comes from the classic three-point rule, which takes the minimum, minimum minus one and minimum plus one, plus the maximum, maximum minus one and maximum plus one, giving six test cases in total [1]. The reasoning is that off-by-one errors cluster at the edges of a range, which is why BVA is usually paired with equivalence partitioning: partitioning picks the classes, and BVA picks the values at their edges [1].

What does branch coverage require for an.raw:
Branch coverage requires every decision to take both its true and false outcome at least once [1]. For an if statement with no else clause, that means one test that skips the body (the false outcome) and one test that enters it (the true outcome) [1].

conditions inside a single decision.

passages.title: Boundary Value Analysis
passages.heading: Boundary value analysis, usually shortened to BVA, is a black-box testing technique
passages.text:
Boundary value analysis, usually shortened to BVA, is a black-box testing technique
that designs test cases around the edges of the input domain. The idea is that
programmers most often make mistakes at the boundaries of a range, such as the
minimum, the maximum, and the values immediately inside and outside them.

For a field that accepts integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA suggests testing the
values 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101. The classic three-point rule tests the minimum, the
minimum minus one and the minimum plus one, plus the maximum, the maximum minus one
and the maximum plus one, which yields six test cases.

BVA pairs naturally with equivalence partitioning. Equivalence partitioning first
divides the input domain into classes of values that should behave the same, and then
boundary value analysis picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one
errors are most likely to hide.

passages.title: Equivalence Partitioning
passages.heading: Equivalence partitioning, or EP, divides the input domain of a program into
passages.text:
Equivalence partitioning, or EP, divides the input domain of a program into
equivalence classes: groups of values the program is expected to treat identically.
Testing one representative value from each class is assumed to reveal the same faults
as testing every member of the class, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases.

Partitions are drawn from both valid and invalid inputs. For an age field that accepts
0 to 120, the valid class is the range 0 to 120, and there are two invalid classes:
negative values and values above 120. A complete test set samples at least one value
from each class.

When a program takes several inputs, EP considers each input's classes independently
and then combines representative values, usually with an all-combinations or pairwise
strategy. The resulting test suite is much smaller than exhaustive testing but still
covers every behaviourally distinct category of input.

passages.title: Statement and Branch Coverage
passages.heading: Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
passages.text:
Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

Branch coverage is often called decision coverage. It subsumes statement coverage:
reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.
